subthemes.text:
OVERVIEW

[1] XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Appellant) appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated August 25, 2020, rejecting his claim for refugee protection because he was found to be excluded pursuant to Section E of Article 1 (Article 1E) of the United Nations Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees (Convention) and section 98 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). The Appellant is a citizen of Ghana and a holder of a United States (US) green card which granted him permanent resident status in that country. The Appellant alleges fear, that if he returned to Ghana, he would be threatened, harmed, or killed based on his sexual orientation. The RPD determined that the Appellant was excluded from refugee protection under Article 1E due to his permanent resident status in the US. The determinative issue in this appeal is whether the RPD erred in its assessment of their exclusion from refugee protection.

[2] In my reasons, I have considered and applied the new Jurisprudential Guide (JG) - Decision MB8-00025 as designated by the Chairperson on December 22, 2020. I agree with the reasoning adopted in the JG regarding the application of Article 1E and as a result, I am applying the "traditional framework of analysis" as outlined in the JG1 to support this decision.
DECISION

[3] I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
ROLE OF THE REFUGEE APPEAL DIVISION (RAD)

[4] My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.2

subthemes.text:
BACKGROUND

[5] On XXXX XXXX, 2011, the Appellant was granted permanent residence in the US. He was issued a green card confirming that status on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2011.3 He maintains a valid green card until XXXX XXXX, 2021.4 On XXXX XXXX, 2012, the Appellant left the US5 to accompany his uncle's body back to Ghana. He remained in Ghana until 2018. He continued his life with his wife he married in 2010, prior to going to the US, and had a daughter in 2014 with a woman that was not his wife. In XXXX 2017, his wife became suspicious and confronted him about his relationship with his same-sex partner XXXX which resulted in his marriage ending in XXXX 2017. In XXXX 2017, he met another woman named XXXX and they started to live together in early 2018. XXXX did not know about his sexual orientation rumours because she lived in a different part of town. On XXXX XXXX, 2018, XXXX called the Appellant to tell him he was wanted by the police because he had been charged with sodomy and homosexuality. His relationship with XXXX ended. He utilized his US green card to gain visitor status in Canada. He left Ghana and arrived in Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2018. He was extended a visitor visa because of his US status. He filed for an extension of the visitor status which was granted. The Appellant made a refugee claim in Canada in fall 2019 and had his eligibility interview on October 9, 2019.

ANALYSIS

[6] In applying the approach of the JG to the circumstances of this case, I find the RPD incorrectly applied the jurisprudence, however, correctly concluded that the Appellant is excluded from refugee protection by the combined effect of Article 1E and s. 98 of the IRPA. The RPD did consider the risk,6 however, the Appellant said he did not actually fear anything so the RPD concluded there was no risk in the US when concluding the Appellant was excluded as part of its Article 1E analysis. Despite quoting the wrong test in its analysis, the RPD correctly assessed risk and concluded that the Appellant would not face a serious possibility of persecution or a likelihood that he would be subjected to danger of torture, a risk to life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in the US. Therefore, the RPD correctly concluded that the Appellant is excluded from refugee protection.

[8] The RPD found the Appellant was excluded pursuant to Article 1E of the Refugee Convention and as such he is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. In coming to that conclusion, the RPD found that due to his lawful status as a permanent resident of the US, he can return and remain there. Furthermore, it found he has the rights and obligations attached to the nationality in that country and he does not have a well-founded fear of persecution in the US. The RPD relied on the Shamloo8 and Wassiq9 to assess whether the Appellant was excluded.

[9] The Appellant submits the RPD applied the wrong legal test in finding the Appellant was excluded. He argues that the correct test is Zeng,10 as set out by the Federal Court of Appeal in 2010.

[10] I note that the Minister intervened before the RPD and relied on Zeng11 in their submissions submitting the Appellant was excluded. The Minister did not intervene before the RAD.

[11] In summary, the RPD did not identify the correct jurisprudence when it did not indicate it would follow the test in Zeng. The RAD finds the correct test to apply is Zeng and applies it to this appeal.
The Appellant has not demonstrated that he does not have valid status in the US

[12] The Appellant had status in the US at the time of the RPD hearing and has not demonstrated that the RPD incorrectly came to that conclusion.

[14] The Appellant submits that he does not have status in the US, substantially similar to that of its nationals, in the US.

[15] Aside from the Appellant's green card that is valid until XXXX 2021,12 the Appellant confirmed in his testimony three important facts: first that he never abandoned his US green card;13 second, that he was never told by any US official that he lost his status in that country;14 and third that he never filed US income tax after leaving the US in 2012.15 He also testified that upon leaving the US in 2012, the Appellant said one of the officers asked him when he would return after he delivered the dead body, so he told them he did not know when he would return to the US. He also told the border officer that he was not sure what he would do after his uncle's funeral at which time he was advised that he had six months to return to the country and if he did not get back by the six months then that visa allowing him to stay would be taken away from him.16

[16] There is also evidence from the US authorities that the Appellant would not be denied entry in the US. The documentary evidence before me also confirms that the US authorities confirmed the Appellant was a permanent resident of the US, was never placed in removal proceedings and/or his status revoked.17 At the time of the Appellant's entry into Canada, the Border Services Officer verified with the US Customs and Border Patrol (USCPB) that the Appellant could proceed to the USA on XXXX XXXX, 2019, by flight. The US authorities confirmed the Appellant would be allowed entry into the USA.18

[17] I turned my attention to the evidence in the legal opinion19 which concluded that the Appellant has abandoned his Lawful Permanent Resident (LPR) status in the US and is not eligible for SB-1 Returning Resident Visa that is made available to returning permanent residents of the US because he remained outside the US for more than a year, he intentionally did not return to the US after his uncle's death as there was no support system made available to him to independently remain as an LPR and the Appellant willingly remained in Ghana without the expectation of returning to the US. Therefore, the legal opinion is that his LPR is deemed abandoned and he does not qualify for any SM-1 Returning Resident Visa as he does not fulfill the above criteria as a returning resident of the US.20 This legal opinion highlights the following sections of the US Foreign Affairs Manual (FAM) which states that an LPR who has remained outside of the US for more than one year may be eligible for status as a returning resident if they satisfy that: 1) Departed the US with the intention of returning to an unrelinquished residence; and 2) the alien's stay abroad was not for reasons beyond his control and for which he was not responsible.21 In addition, this document also states that the US authorities instructions on Maintaining Permanent Residence states:
"You may be found to have abandoned your status if:
Move to another country, intending to live there permanently; remain outside of the United States for an extended period of time, unless intended to be a temporary absence, as shown by:
* the reason for your trip; how long you intended to be absent from the United States;
* any other circumstances of your absence; and any events that may have prolonged your absence.
* Note: Obtaining a re-entry from USCIS before you leave, or a returning resident visa (SB-1) from a U.S. consulate while abroad, may assist you in showing that you intended only a temporary absence.
* Fail to file income tax returns while living outside of the United States for any period.
* Declare yourself a "nonimmigrant" on your U.S. tax returns."22 [underline added]
The legal opinion further proposes, in addition to the 9 FAM 502.7-2, the Applicant seeking an SB-1 visa must provide evidence of Intent to Return to Unrelinquished Residence in the US. It suggests that the evidence must demonstrate the following:
* Was a lawfully admitted permanent resident of the United States at the time of departure;
* At the time of departure, had the intention of returning to the United States;
* While residing abroad, did not abandon the intention to return to the United States; and
* Is returning from a temporary residence abroad; or if the stay was protracted, this was caused by reasons beyond the alien's control.23

subthemes.text:
[18] The objective evidence in the National Documentation Package (NDP) for the US24 states that according to the website of the United States Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) once a person becomes an LPR, also known as a green card holder, LPR is maintained until the person applies and completes the naturalization process or until the LPR status is lost or abandoned. The USCIS also states that a person "will lose [their] permanent resident status if an immigration judge issues a final removal order" against them or an individual "may lose" their LPR by intentionally abandoning it, or, the person may be found to have abandoned their status by: moving to another country with the intention of living there permanently; failing to file income tax while living outside the US for any period of time; declaring oneself a "nonimmigration" on one's US tax returns. More importantly, this evidence states: according to the website of the Chodorow Law Offices, which is a law firm based in Beijing specializing in US immigration matters, "if it appears [that a person has] abandoned [their] LPR status and [they] are not willing to voluntarily give it up, the [Customs and Border Protection, CPB] officer may refer [the person] to the Immigration Court for a judge to determine whether [the person has] lost [their] status.25

[19] As per the facts, I find that the Appellant has not abandoned his LPR himself and the objective evidence supports him losing his LPR is not automatic. The Appellant has not demonstrated he is deemed to have lost his LPR in the US. There is conflicting evidence before me as to whether the Appellant would be allowed re-entry to the US. Based on what is before me, I place more weight on the evidence from the US authorities that demonstrates that the Appellant would not be denied entry in the US, and that the Appellant has never tried to do so which further supports the objective evidence noted above. Given the Appellant has never voluntarily abandoned his LPR; he was never told by any US official that he lost his status in that country and that there is a process in the US for him to seek to re-enter the US and an opportunity to maintain his permanent resident status in the US with the rights and freedoms that go along with that. I also do not accept the Appellant's testimony to be credible that when he left the US, the Border authorities told him that if he remained outside of the country for more than six months, he would lose it because this is not consistent with the legal opinion that an LPR holder who has remained outside of the US for more than one year may be eligible for returning resident status. The Appellant has not demonstrated, on the balance of probabilities, that the US would not allow him entry. At the time of the RPD hearing, the Appellant had LPR status in the US which he happens to maintain at appeal. There is no indication that residency shall be revoked if the Appellant is absent for a specific period or that the decision is automatic. In my view, there is a process in place for him to access in the US, and that process has not been exhausted which leads me to conclude he maintains an LPR in the US and therefore he has the rights and obligations which are attached to the possession of that status in the US. In summary, I find the Appellant had valid legal status in the US at the time of the RPD hearing and in fact continues to do so until XXXX 2021.
The RPD assessed and concluded that the Appellant does not face risk or fear in the US by his own admission

It correctly concluded that the Appellant does not face a risk or fear in the US. The evidence before the RPD and I is clear, the Appellant did not present any risk or harm to him in the US. In this case, the Appellant faces no fear in the US by his own admission. The RPD did not need to continue any further once it came to that conclusion and the RAD need not either. The RPD correctly concluded that the Appellant as an LPR of the US that he could return to that country of residence without facing any fear.

[13] The RPD found that the Appellant does have status similar to that of its nationals in the US.

[14] The Appellant submits that he does not have status in the US, substantially similar to that of its nationals, in the US.

[15] Aside from the Appellant's green card that is valid until XXXX 2021,12 the Appellant confirmed in his testimony three important facts: first that he never abandoned his US green card;13 second, that he was never told by any US official that he lost his status in that country;14 and third that he never filed US income tax after leaving the US in 2012.15 He also testified that upon leaving the US in 2012, the Appellant said one of the officers asked him when he would return after he delivered the dead body, so he told them he did not know when he would return to the US. He also told the border officer that he was not sure what he would do after his uncle's funeral at which time he was advised that he had six months to return to the country and if he did not get back by the six months then that visa allowing him to stay would be taken away from him.16

[16] There is also evidence from the US authorities that the Appellant would not be denied entry in the US. The documentary evidence before me also confirms that the US authorities confirmed the Appellant was a permanent resident of the US, was never placed in removal proceedings and/or his status revoked.17 At the time of the Appellant's entry into Canada, the Border Services Officer verified with the US Customs and Border Patrol (USCPB) that the Appellant could proceed to the USA on XXXX XXXX, 2019, by flight. The US authorities confirmed the Appellant would be allowed entry into the USA.18

[17] I turned my attention to the evidence in the legal opinion19 which concluded that the Appellant has abandoned his Lawful Permanent Resident (LPR) status in the US and is not eligible for SB-1 Returning Resident Visa that is made available to returning permanent residents of the US because he remained outside the US for more than a year, he intentionally did not return to the US after his uncle's death as there was no support system made available to him to independently remain as an LPR and the Appellant willingly remained in Ghana without the expectation of returning to the US. Therefore, the legal opinion is that his LPR is deemed abandoned and he does not qualify for any SM-1 Returning Resident Visa as he does not fulfill the above criteria as a returning resident of the US.20 This legal opinion highlights the following sections of the US Foreign Affairs Manual (FAM) which states that an LPR who has remained outside of the US for more than one year may be eligible for status as a returning resident if they satisfy that: 1) Departed the US with the intention of returning to an unrelinquished residence; and 2) the alien's stay abroad was not for reasons beyond his control and for which he was not responsible.21 In addition, this document also states that the US authorities instructions on Maintaining Permanent Residence states:
"You may be found to have abandoned your status if:
Move to another country, intending to live there permanently; remain outside of the United States for an extended period of time, unless intended to be a temporary absence, as shown by:
* the reason for your trip; how long you intended to be absent from the United States;
* any other circumstances of your absence; and any events that may have prolonged your absence.
* Note: Obtaining a re-entry from USCIS before you leave, or a returning resident visa (SB-1) from a U.S. consulate while abroad, may assist you in showing that you intended only a temporary absence.
* Fail to file income tax returns while living outside of the United States for any period.
* Declare yourself a "nonimmigrant" on your U.S. tax returns."22 [underline added]
The legal opinion further proposes, in addition to the 9 FAM 502.7-2, the Applicant seeking an SB-1 visa must provide evidence of Intent to Return to Unrelinquished Residence in the US. It suggests that the evidence must demonstrate the following:
* Was a lawfully admitted permanent resident of the United States at the time of departure;
* At the time of departure, had the intention of returning to the United States;
* While residing abroad, did not abandon the intention to return to the United States; and
* Is returning from a temporary residence abroad; or if the stay was protracted, this was caused by reasons beyond the alien's control.23

[18] The objective evidence in the National Documentation Package (NDP) for the US24 states that according to the website of the United States Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) once a person becomes an LPR, also known as a green card holder, LPR is maintained until the person applies and completes the naturalization process or until the LPR status is lost or abandoned. The USCIS also states that a person "will lose [their] permanent resident status if an immigration judge issues a final removal order" against them or an individual "may lose" their LPR by intentionally abandoning it, or, the person may be found to have abandoned their status by: moving to another country with the intention of living there permanently; failing to file income tax while living outside the US for any period of time; declaring oneself a "nonimmigration" on one's US tax returns. More importantly, this evidence states: according to the website of the Chodorow Law Offices, which is a law firm based in Beijing specializing in US immigration matters, "if it appears [that a person has] abandoned [their] LPR status and [they] are not willing to voluntarily give it up, the [Customs and Border Protection, CPB] officer may refer [the person] to the Immigration Court for a judge to determine whether [the person has] lost [their] status.25

[19] As per the facts, I find that the Appellant has not abandoned his LPR himself and the objective evidence supports him losing his LPR is not automatic. The Appellant has not demonstrated he is deemed to have lost his LPR in the US. There is conflicting evidence before me as to whether the Appellant would be allowed re-entry to the US. Based on what is before me, I place more weight on the evidence from the US authorities that demonstrates that the Appellant would not be denied entry in the US, and that the Appellant has never tried to do so which further supports the objective evidence noted above. Given the Appellant has never voluntarily abandoned his LPR; he was never told by any US official that he lost his status in that country and that there is a process in the US for him to seek to re-enter the US and an opportunity to maintain his permanent resident status in the US with the rights and freedoms that go along with that. I also do not accept the Appellant's testimony to be credible that when he left the US, the Border authorities told him that if he remained outside of the country for more than six months, he would lose it because this is not consistent with the legal opinion that an LPR holder who has remained outside of the US for more than one year may be eligible for returning resident status. The Appellant has not demonstrated, on the balance of probabilities, that the US would not allow him entry. At the time of the RPD hearing, the Appellant had LPR status in the US which he happens to maintain at appeal. There is no indication that residency shall be revoked if the Appellant is absent for a specific period or that the decision is automatic. In my view, there is a process in place for him to access in the US, and that process has not been exhausted which leads me to conclude he maintains an LPR in the US and therefore he has the rights and obligations which are attached to the possession of that status in the US. In summary, I find the Appellant had valid legal status in the US at the time of the RPD hearing and in fact continues to do so until XXXX 2021.
The RPD assessed and concluded that the Appellant does not face risk or fear in the US by his own admission

[20] With my finding that the Appellant has status in a country of residence, substantially similar to that of its nationals in the US, I turn to whether the Appellant's country of residence is unsafe for him to return to, namely whether he would he face a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground or, the likelihood of being subjected to a danger of torture, a risk to life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment for which he would have no state protection or internal flight alternative. Based on the Appellant's own admission, I find he will not face risk or fear should he return to the US. As such, the Appellant is excluded.

[21] The RPD considered the Appellant's risk or fear in the US and it provided its conclusion on risk or fear in its reasons. Namely, that the Appellant had none by his own admission.

[22] The Appellant submits the RPD erred by not clearly outlining the Zeng26 test or moving on to part two and three of Zeng.

[23] I find the RPD did assess the risk or fear in the US in paragraph 25 of its reasons for decision. It was just a cursory analysis because there was nothing factually to evaluate. It correctly concluded that the Appellant does not face a risk or fear in the US. The evidence before the RPD and I is clear, the Appellant did not present any risk or harm to him in the US. Following the test in Zeng, I conclude based on the Appellant's testimony,27 that he would not face any fear in the US. Again, when there's nothing factual to evaluate, the RAD like the RPD need only consider the evidence the Appellant presented and make a finding on that factual evidence. In this case, the Appellant faces no fear in the US by his own admission. The RPD did not need to continue any further once it came to that conclusion and the RAD need not either. The RPD correctly concluded that the Appellant as an LPR of the US that he could return to that country of residence without facing any fear.

REASONS FOR DECISION
OVERVIEW

[1] XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Appellant) appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated August 25, 2020, rejecting his claim for refugee protection because he was found to be excluded pursuant to Section E of Article 1 (Article 1E) of the United Nations Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees (Convention) and section 98 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). The Appellant is a citizen of Ghana and a holder of a United States (US) green card which granted him permanent resident status in that country. The Appellant alleges fear, that if he returned to Ghana, he would be threatened, harmed, or killed based on his sexual orientation. The RPD determined that the Appellant was excluded from refugee protection under Article 1E due to his permanent resident status in the US. The determinative issue in this appeal is whether the RPD erred in its assessment of their exclusion from refugee protection.

[2] In my reasons, I have considered and applied the new Jurisprudential Guide (JG) - Decision MB8-00025 as designated by the Chairperson on December 22, 2020. I agree with the reasoning adopted in the JG regarding the application of Article 1E and as a result, I am applying the "traditional framework of analysis" as outlined in the JG1 to support this decision.
DECISION

[3] I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
ROLE OF THE REFUGEE APPEAL DIVISION (RAD)
[4] My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.2
BACKGROUND

[5] On XXXX XXXX, 2011, the Appellant was granted permanent residence in the US. He was issued a green card confirming that status on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2011.3 He maintains a valid green card until XXXX XXXX, 2021.4 On XXXX XXXX, 2012, the Appellant left the US5 to accompany his uncle's body back to Ghana. He remained in Ghana until 2018. He continued his life with his wife he married in 2010, prior to going to the US, and had a daughter in 2014 with a woman that was not his wife. In XXXX 2017, his wife became suspicious and confronted him about his relationship with his same-sex partner XXXX which resulted in his marriage ending in XXXX 2017. In XXXX 2017, he met another woman named XXXX and they started to live together in early 2018. XXXX did not know about his sexual orientation rumours because she lived in a different part of town. On XXXX XXXX, 2018, XXXX called the Appellant to tell him he was wanted by the police because he had been charged with sodomy and homosexuality. His relationship with XXXX ended. He utilized his US green card to gain visitor status in Canada. He left Ghana and arrived in Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2018. He was extended a visitor visa because of his US status. He filed for an extension of the visitor status which was granted. The Appellant made a refugee claim in Canada in fall 2019 and had his eligibility interview on October 9, 2019.
ANALYSIS

[6] In applying the approach of the JG to the circumstances of this case, I find the RPD incorrectly applied the jurisprudence, however, correctly concluded that the Appellant is excluded from refugee protection by the combined effect of Article 1E and s. 98 of the IRPA. The RPD did consider the risk,6 however, the Appellant said he did not actually fear anything so the RPD concluded there was no risk in the US when concluding the Appellant was excluded as part of its Article 1E analysis. Despite quoting the wrong test in its analysis, the RPD correctly assessed risk and concluded that the Appellant would not face a serious possibility of persecution or a likelihood that he would be subjected to danger of torture, a risk to life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in the US. Therefore, the RPD correctly concluded that the Appellant is excluded from refugee protection.
Correct jurisprudence applied by RAD
[7] I follow the Majebi7 decision and agree with the RPD evaluation that at the time of the hearing that the Appellant had valid permanent resident status in the US.

[8] The RPD found the Appellant was excluded pursuant to Article 1E of the Refugee Convention and as such he is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. In coming to that conclusion, the RPD found that due to his lawful status as a permanent resident of the US, he can return and remain there. Furthermore, it found he has the rights and obligations attached to the nationality in that country and he does not have a well-founded fear of persecution in the US. The RPD relied on the Shamloo8 and Wassiq9 to assess whether the Appellant was excluded.
[9] The Appellant submits the RPD applied the wrong legal test in finding the Appellant was excluded. He argues that the correct test is Zeng,10 as set out by the Federal Court of Appeal in 2010.
[10] I note that the Minister intervened before the RPD and relied on Zeng11 in their submissions submitting the Appellant was excluded. The Minister did not intervene before the RAD.

[11] In summary, the RPD did not identify the correct jurisprudence when it did not indicate it would follow the test in Zeng. The RAD finds the correct test to apply is Zeng and applies it to this appeal.
The Appellant has not demonstrated that he does not have valid status in the US
[12] The Appellant had status in the US at the time of the RPD hearing and has not demonstrated that the RPD incorrectly came to that conclusion.
[13] The RPD found that the Appellant does have status similar to that of its nationals in the US.
[14] The Appellant submits that he does not have status in the US, substantially similar to that of its nationals, in the US.

[15] Aside from the Appellant's green card that is valid until XXXX 2021,12 the Appellant confirmed in his testimony three important facts: first that he never abandoned his US green card;13 second, that he was never told by any US official that he lost his status in that country;14 and third that he never filed US income tax after leaving the US in 2012.15 He also testified that upon leaving the US in 2012, the Appellant said one of the officers asked him when he would return after he delivered the dead body, so he told them he did not know when he would return to the US. He also told the border officer that he was not sure what he would do after his uncle's funeral at which time he was advised that he had six months to return to the country and if he did not get back by the six months then that visa allowing him to stay would be taken away from him.16

[16] There is also evidence from the US authorities that the Appellant would not be denied entry in the US. The documentary evidence before me also confirms that the US authorities confirmed the Appellant was a permanent resident of the US, was never placed in removal proceedings and/or his status revoked.17 At the time of the Appellant's entry into Canada, the Border Services Officer verified with the US Customs and Border Patrol (USCPB) that the Appellant could proceed to the USA on XXXX XXXX, 2019, by flight. The US authorities confirmed the Appellant would be allowed entry into the USA.18

[17] I turned my attention to the evidence in the legal opinion19 which concluded that the Appellant has abandoned his Lawful Permanent Resident (LPR) status in the US and is not eligible for SB-1 Returning Resident Visa that is made available to returning permanent residents of the US because he remained outside the US for more than a year, he intentionally did not return to the US after his uncle's death as there was no support system made available to him to independently remain as an LPR and the Appellant willingly remained in Ghana without the expectation of returning to the US. Therefore, the legal opinion is that his LPR is deemed abandoned and he does not qualify for any SM-1 Returning Resident Visa as he does not fulfill the above criteria as a returning resident of the US.20 This legal opinion highlights the following sections of the US Foreign Affairs Manual (FAM) which states that an LPR who has remained outside of the US for more than one year may be eligible for status as a returning resident if they satisfy that: 1) Departed the US with the intention of returning to an unrelinquished residence; and 2) the alien's stay abroad was not for reasons beyond his control and for which he was not responsible.21 In addition, this document also states that the US authorities instructions on Maintaining Permanent Residence states:
"You may be found to have abandoned your status if:
Move to another country, intending to live there permanently; remain outside of the United States for an extended period of time, unless intended to be a temporary absence, as shown by:
* the reason for your trip; how long you intended to be absent from the United States;
* any other circumstances of your absence; and any events that may have prolonged your absence.
* Note: Obtaining a re-entry from USCIS before you leave, or a returning resident visa (SB-1) from a U.S. consulate while abroad, may assist you in showing that you intended only a temporary absence.
* Fail to file income tax returns while living outside of the United States for any period.
* Declare yourself a "nonimmigrant" on your U.S. tax returns."22 [underline added]
The legal opinion further proposes, in addition to the 9 FAM 502.7-2, the Applicant seeking an SB-1 visa must provide evidence of Intent to Return to Unrelinquished Residence in the US. It suggests that the evidence must demonstrate the following:
* Was a lawfully admitted permanent resident of the United States at the time of departure;
* At the time of departure, had the intention of returning to the United States;
* While residing abroad, did not abandon the intention to return to the United States; and
* Is returning from a temporary residence abroad; or if the stay was protracted, this was caused by reasons beyond the alien's control.23

[18] The objective evidence in the National Documentation Package (NDP) for the US24 states that according to the website of the United States Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) once a person becomes an LPR, also known as a green card holder, LPR is maintained until the person applies and completes the naturalization process or until the LPR status is lost or abandoned. The USCIS also states that a person "will lose [their] permanent resident status if an immigration judge issues a final removal order" against them or an individual "may lose" their LPR by intentionally abandoning it, or, the person may be found to have abandoned their status by: moving to another country with the intention of living there permanently; failing to file income tax while living outside the US for any period of time; declaring oneself a "nonimmigration" on one's US tax returns. More importantly, this evidence states: according to the website of the Chodorow Law Offices, which is a law firm based in Beijing specializing in US immigration matters, "if it appears [that a person has] abandoned [their] LPR status and [they] are not willing to voluntarily give it up, the [Customs and Border Protection, CPB] officer may refer [the person] to the Immigration Court for a judge to determine whether [the person has] lost [their] status.25

[19] As per the facts, I find that the Appellant has not abandoned his LPR himself and the objective evidence supports him losing his LPR is not automatic. The Appellant has not demonstrated he is deemed to have lost his LPR in the US. There is conflicting evidence before me as to whether the Appellant would be allowed re-entry to the US. Based on what is before me, I place more weight on the evidence from the US authorities that demonstrates that the Appellant would not be denied entry in the US, and that the Appellant has never tried to do so which further supports the objective evidence noted above. Given the Appellant has never voluntarily abandoned his LPR; he was never told by any US official that he lost his status in that country and that there is a process in the US for him to seek to re-enter the US and an opportunity to maintain his permanent resident status in the US with the rights and freedoms that go along with that. I also do not accept the Appellant's testimony to be credible that when he left the US, the Border authorities told him that if he remained outside of the country for more than six months, he would lose it because this is not consistent with the legal opinion that an LPR holder who has remained outside of the US for more than one year may be eligible for returning resident status. The Appellant has not demonstrated, on the balance of probabilities, that the US would not allow him entry. At the time of the RPD hearing, the Appellant had LPR status in the US which he happens to maintain at appeal. There is no indication that residency shall be revoked if the Appellant is absent for a specific period or that the decision is automatic. In my view, there is a process in place for him to access in the US, and that process has not been exhausted which leads me to conclude he maintains an LPR in the US and therefore he has the rights and obligations which are attached to the possession of that status in the US. In summary, I find the Appellant had valid legal status in the US at the time of the RPD hearing and in fact continues to do so until XXXX 2021.
The RPD assessed and concluded that the Appellant does not face risk or fear in the US by his own admission

[20] With my finding that the Appellant has status in a country of residence, substantially similar to that of its nationals in the US, I turn to whether the Appellant's country of residence is unsafe for him to return to, namely whether he would he face a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground or, the likelihood of being subjected to a danger of torture, a risk to life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment for which he would have no state protection or internal flight alternative. Based on the Appellant's own admission, I find he will not face risk or fear should he return to the US. As such, the Appellant is excluded.
[21] The RPD considered the Appellant's risk or fear in the US and it provided its conclusion on risk or fear in its reasons. Namely, that the Appellant had none by his own admission.
[22] The Appellant submits the RPD erred by not clearly outlining the Zeng26 test or moving on to part two and three of Zeng.

[23] I find the RPD did assess the risk or fear in the US in paragraph 25 of its reasons for decision. It was just a cursory analysis because there was nothing factually to evaluate. It correctly concluded that the Appellant does not face a risk or fear in the US. The evidence before the RPD and I is clear, the Appellant did not present any risk or harm to him in the US. Following the test in Zeng, I conclude based on the Appellant's testimony,27 that he would not face any fear in the US. Again, when there's nothing factual to evaluate, the RAD like the RPD need only consider the evidence the Appellant presented and make a finding on that factual evidence. In this case, the Appellant faces no fear in the US by his own admission. The RPD did not need to continue any further once it came to that conclusion and the RAD need not either. The RPD correctly concluded that the Appellant as an LPR of the US that he could return to that country of residence without facing any fear.
CONCLUSION

[24] For the above reasons, I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that XXXX XXXX XXXX is excluded from refugee protection by the combined effect of Article 1E of the Convention and section 98 of the IRPA.
(signed)
Julie Ryan
Julie Ryan
June 3, 2021
